text: The Hadley house stood at the high end of the avenue, white and indifferent behind its rows of clipped privet, and on summer nights it shed light the way a careless woman sheds compliments. I went there first in July, when the lawns were still wet from the sprinklers and the orchestra had not yet learned the tune it would play until October. Vivian Hadley received her guests from the foot of the marble stair, a champagne flute tilted in her gloved hand, and she had the particular gift of making each arrival feel like the one she had been waiting for all evening. It was a lie, of course, but a generous lie, the kind that costs the teller nothing and warms the listener for a week. The men in their summer flannels talked of yachts they meant to buy and women they meant to forget, and the girls laughed at things that were not funny because laughter was the currency of the season. I stood at the edge of the terrace and watched the moon lay a silver road across the Sound, and I understood, with the clean sad certainty that comes only once or twice in a life, that all of this brightness was borrowed, and that the lender was already at the gate.

Clara wore green that autumn, a green like the underside of a leaf turning, and she moved through the Plaza ballroom as though the floor had been laid expressly for her feet. I had loved her in a thin, hopeful way for three years, the way a poor man loves a house he passes on his walk home, and I had told myself that nearness would be enough. It is never enough. She danced with a broad-shouldered boy from Yale who would inherit a railroad and a face that had never been refused anything, and when she passed me she smiled the smile she gave to waiters and to weather. The chandeliers burned above us like small captured suns, and the music was the kind that promises everything and remembers nothing. Later, on the steps, she touched my sleeve and said she was glad I had come, and for a moment the whole gaudy night narrowed to that warm gloved hand. Then a motorcar drew up, and she was gone into the lamplit dark with her railroad boy, and I walked back through the empty park alone. We spend our youth believing the door will open if we only knock politely enough. The cruelty is not that it stays shut. The cruelty is that we keep our hand raised long after the house has gone dark.

Tommy Vane came home from Paris in the spring of twenty-four with a tan, a wife, and the unmistakable air of a man who has spent more than he owns. We had been roommates once, in the lean honest years before the world went golden, and I remembered him eating crackers in the dark and swearing he would one day dine on the moon. Now he dined everywhere, signed everything, and laughed too quickly at his own remarks. His wife, Renee, was beautiful in the expensive, brittle way of cut crystal, and she watched him across the dinner table with an expression I could not at first name, until I saw it was the look of a woman counting the days of a thing she had not yet admitted was ending. They had a villa, a roadster the color of butter, and a calendar full of weekends that all ran together into one long shimmering Saturday. I envied them for exactly the length of one cocktail. Then Tommy laughed again, and I heard underneath it the small dry rattle of a man who has discovered that the moon, once reached, is only cold stone after all. The trouble with getting everything you wanted is that it leaves you nothing to want, and a man without wanting is a clock without hands, beautiful and useless and exactly on time for nothing.

There was a girl named June Carrow whom everyone agreed would marry magnificently, and for a while the agreement seemed to be merely a description of the inevitable. She had hair the color of late wheat and a laugh that made strangers turn in restaurants, and she carried her beauty the way a soldier carries a flag in peacetime, proudly and without quite knowing what it was for. The summer she was nineteen she had four proposals and refused them all, because refusal was still a luxury she could afford, like the orchids she let wilt unworn upon her dresser. I saw her last at a wedding that was not her own, in a gown a season out of fashion, smiling at the bride with a brightness sharpened by something it had cost her to summon. The band played the songs of five years before, and the older men remembered when she had been the one the whole room watched. Beauty, I have come to think, is a kind of credit extended by the young against a future they assume will pay. June had spent hers freely, magnificently, on nothing in particular, and now the account was closing in the slow polite way that accounts do, and there was nobody left at the window to mark the final, quiet withdrawal.

The last party of the season was always held at the Endicotts', when the maples had begun to rust and the Sound had taken on the gray of an old mirror. By then the summer people were tired in the way that pleasure makes you tired, hollowed and luminous, and they came to dance the final dances with a desperate gaiety that fooled no one and comforted everyone. I found old Endicott on the veranda near midnight, a cigar gone cold in his fingers, watching the young people whirl past the lighted windows. He had been rich for forty years and had buried two wives and one fortune, and he said to me, without turning, that the music sounded exactly as it had in eighteen ninety-nine, and that this was the saddest thing he knew. Inside, a girl in silver was being kissed in a doorway by a boy who would not write to her, and both of them believed, for that single suspended moment, that the night would never have to end. It always ends. The cars come round at two, the lanterns gutter, the orchestra packs its brass into worn velvet cases. And we drive home along the dark coast road, each of us privately certain that next summer the lights will burn a little brighter, knowing in the same breath that they never do.
